findings.message: `updateItem` never calls `setActivities`. Both `addItem` (line 38) and `deleteItem` (line 74) push an `ActivityEntry` after mutating items, but `updateItem` only calls `setItems`. The `ActivityEntry` type even declares an `'updated'` action for this purpose. After editing an item, the activity feed on the dashboard is never updated, making edits invisible to audit history.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: updateItem only calls setItems with no setActivities call, while addItem and deleteItem both push ActivityEntry records. The ActivityEntry type has an 'updated' action variant that is never used. Edits made via the new UI path produce no activity log entry.
findings.severity_justification: The activity/audit feed on the dashboard will silently omit all item edits — a meaningful gap in the audit trail, but not data loss or a broken core workflow.
findings.category_justification: Incomplete implementation of a feature: the update path skips the side-effect (activity logging) that the other two mutation paths consistently apply.

findings.message: When `editItem` is provided but `onUpdate` is `undefined`, the condition `isEditMode && editItem && onUpdate` is falsy and the `else` branch fires, calling `onAdd(form)`. This creates a duplicate inventory entry instead of updating the original. Since `onUpdate` is typed as optional (`onUpdate?:`), this is a reachable failure path. The two props should be paired with a discriminated type or `onUpdate` made required whenever `editItem` is present.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: both editItem and onUpdate are typed as optional in AddItemModalProps, and the handleSubmit guard falls through to onAdd when editItem is present but onUpdate is absent. The current call site always passes both, so it's not triggered today, but the type contract does not enforce the pairing and the silent fallback to onAdd is a real hazard.
findings.severity_justification: Not currently triggered at the only call site, but the type design allows callers to provide editItem without onUpdate and silently get duplicate-item creation instead of an update.
findings.category_justification: Root issue is type design: two props that must co-occur are independently optional with no discriminated union or other enforcement, creating an unsafe public interface.

findings.message: The `useState` initializer captures `editItem` at mount time, which is correct when the key-remount mechanism is used. However, the component is also mounted invisibly (key=0, `isOpen=false`) on initial page load before any modal is opened. This is a design coupling — the form reset behaviour is entirely dependent on the parent always calling `openModal()` (which increments the key) rather than setting `isModalOpen` directly. If any future caller sets `isOpen` to true without changing the key, the stale state from a previous session is silently used.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the form reset depends entirely on key-based remounting, which only occurs inside openModal(). If isModalOpen is set to true by any path that doesn't increment modalKey, stale form state is reused silently. The coupling is real, though the current code has only one call site that always goes through openModal().
findings.severity_justification: Not a current bug — all open paths go through openModal() which always increments the key. The risk is future-caller fragility only, and the component is used in exactly one place.
findings.category_justification: The issue is a design coupling and implicit contract between the parent and child: form reset correctness depends on the parent always going through a specific helper function rather than being enforced at the component boundary.

findings.message: The new delete-activity test covers the newly added test case, but there is no corresponding test for `updateItem` creating an activity entry — which it never does (see `useInventory.ts` lines 43–55). The PR claims to 'Complete the Update path' but neither the hook nor the test suite captures or verifies the activity side-effect for updates.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: no test asserts that updateItem creates an ActivityEntry. The existing 'updates an item' test only checks quantity and status. updateItem has no setActivities call, so such a test would currently fail — but the gap in test coverage is real and independently actionable.
findings.severity_justification: The underlying implementation gap (missing activity logging) is the primary issue; the missing test is a secondary symptom. Low severity as a standalone test-coverage finding since fixing the hook (Finding 1) would make this test straightforward to add.
findings.category_justification: The finding specifically identifies a missing test case for the update activity side-effect, which is a test coverage gap distinct from the implementation issue.

findings.message: `deleteItem` calls `setActivities` inside the `setItems` updater function. Calling one state setter inside another's updater is an anti-pattern: the inner `setActivities` call is dispatched during React's reconciliation of the outer `setItems` update, which can cause ordering and batching surprises. Both state transitions should be dispatched at the same level (i.e., read the item to delete first, then call both setters at the top level of the callback). This is pre-existing but the new delete-activity test now relies on this behaviour being reliable.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: deleteItem calls setActivities inside setItems's updater function, a side effect inside a pure updater. The app runs in StrictMode (confirmed in main.tsx), which double-invokes updater functions in development, causing setActivities to fire twice per delete in dev mode. The new test uses renderHook without StrictMode so it passes, masking the issue.
findings.severity_justification: In production the anti-pattern works correctly (one activity entry per delete). The double-invocation issue only surfaces in development/StrictMode, creating duplicate activity entries in the dev UI but not affecting production correctness.
findings.category_justification: The issue concerns React's StrictMode execution model and state-update batching — a runtime behavior concern rather than a logic error or type issue.

findings.message: The test asserts that the new activity entry is at index 0, but `useInventory` prepends new activities to an existing list of mock activities. The test may pass initially if run in isolation, but it's not robust. It should find the new activity in the activities array instead of assuming its position.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The implementation always prepends new activities ([activity, ...prevAct]), so activities[0] deterministically refers to the most recently added entry. Each renderHook call gives a fresh hook instance with only one mutation performed, making the index-0 assertion correct and reliable. The finding mischaracterizes a reliable pattern as fragile.
findings.severity_justification: The finding identifies no actual test fragility — the assertion is correct given the prepend semantics of the hook.
findings.category_justification: The claim is about test assertion robustness.

findings.message: Using a `key` prop to force a remount is a valid strategy to reset state, but it can be inefficient and is often a sign of a component doing too much. A more conventional approach would be to use an effect (`useEffect`) inside `AddItemModal` to reset the form state when `isOpen` changes from `true` to `false`, or when the `editItem` prop changes.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The key-based remount for form reset is the approach explicitly recommended by the React team (documented in 'You Might Not Need an Effect'). The suggested useEffect alternative is what React's docs advise against for state reset: it causes an extra render with stale state visible before the effect fires. The finding recommends a less correct approach as if it were more conventional.
findings.severity_justification: Even if the finding were correct, this would be a style/architecture preference with no behavioral impact.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about component design approach and code organization.

findings.message: When submitting the form in edit mode, the component calls `onUpdate(editItem.id, form)`. However, the `onUpdate` prop expects the second argument to be `Partial<Omit<InventoryItem, 'id'>>`. The `form` state is of type `NewItemData`, which matches `Omit<InventoryItem, 'id' | 'status' | 'lastUpdated'>`. This is compatible, but it means that all fields are being passed in the update, not just the ones that have changed. This could be inefficient if `onUpdate` triggers a full re-render or a network request with the complete object.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The type observation is correct but the stated concern (inefficiency from passing all fields) is hypothetical and does not apply: the hook is purely in-memory with no network layer, and setItems triggers a re-render regardless of update shape. The finding's own 'if' framing acknowledges no actual problem exists in this codebase.
findings.severity_justification: Even if valid, the codebase has no network layer and the performance difference of partial vs full object merging in an in-memory React hook is negligible.
findings.category_justification: The finding's stated concern is about efficiency of passing full objects vs only changed fields.

findings.message: The delete item test assumes there is at least one item initialized in the inventory without validating this precondition, potentially failing if the assumption doesn't hold.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The mock data is hardcoded with 18 items so items[0] is never undefined. The identical pattern of accessing items[0] without an explicit precondition check already exists in the pre-existing 'deletes an item' test. This is a generic defensive-coding suggestion with no realistic failure path in this codebase.
findings.severity_justification: No realistic failure path exists given static hardcoded mock data; the concern is purely theoretical.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about a missing precondition assertion in a test.

findings.message: The default behavior for the quantity and price fields to parse empty input as zero may lead to unintentional overwrites.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: parseInt('',10)||0 evaluates to 0 and parseFloat('')||0 evaluates to 0. In edit mode introduced by this PR, clearing either numeric field and submitting silently overwrites the original non-zero value with 0. For quantity this also triggers status recalculation via deriveStatus, potentially marking an in-stock item as Out of Stock.
findings.severity_justification: Requires the user to clear a numeric field and submit without re-entering a value — not an automatic failure, but silent zero-overwrite of price or quantity is a real data correctness hazard that is worse in edit mode than add mode.
findings.category_justification: The behavior produces incorrect data when a user clears a numeric field during an edit, overwriting valid inventory values with zero.

findings.message: The current implementation of the `onEdit` and `onDelete` event handlers lacks null or undefined checks on `item` and `id`, respectively, which could lead to runtime errors if invalid or unexpected data is passed.
findings.tp_fp_justification: item is the loop variable from items.map() over a typed InventoryItem[] — it is never null/undefined within that callback. item.id is typed as a required string in InventoryItem. There is no external/untyped data source where invalid values could enter. The finding is a generic defensive-null-check suggestion that does not identify a concrete failure path.
findings.severity_justification: Even if taken seriously, no realistic code path exists where item or item.id could be null/undefined given the fully typed in-memory data flow.
findings.category_justification: The finding frames itself as a runtime error risk from missing null checks.

findings.message: Saving from the newly wired edit path will not show up in Recent Activity: this calls `updateItem`, but `useInventory.updateItem` only mutates `items` and never appends an `action: 'updated'` entry, even though add/delete do and the dashboard renders updated activities. Users can now edit items from the UI without any audit/activity record.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed in useInventory.ts: `updateItem` only calls `setItems` and never appends to `activities`, while `addItem` and `deleteItem` both create and prepend an `ActivityEntry`. With the edit path now wired to the UI by this PR, users can edit items with no audit trail record appearing in Recent Activity.
findings.severity_justification: The activity feed is a visible dashboard feature; edits silently go unrecorded while adds and deletes are tracked. It's a functional gap that breaks audit consistency, though it doesn't corrupt data or block the primary workflow.
findings.category_justification: The hook's `updateItem` is inconsistent with the established pattern of recording side-effects in the activity log — it's a logic gap causing incorrect/incomplete behavior relative to the described intent.
